note.explanation: A steel bar can be magnetised by stroking it with a permanent magnet or by placing it inside a solenoid carrying direct current. A magnet can be demagnetised by strong heating, hammering, or slowly moving it out of a solenoid carrying alternating current.
examples: In single-touch stroking, stroke the bar several times in the same direction with the same pole, lifting the magnet at the end of each stroke.
To demagnetise a magnet using A.C., place it inside a long solenoid carrying alternating current and move it out slowly.
note.checkAnswer: Use the right-hand grip rule: curl the fingers in the direction of current in the solenoid; the thumb points towards the bar's N-pole end.
note.simple: Magnetising lines up the magnetic domains in a steel bar. Heating or hammering disturbs their alignment; A.C. in a solenoid can also demagnetise a magnet as it is slowly withdrawn.
note.checkQuestion: How do you find which end of a steel bar is its N-pole when it is inside a current-carrying solenoid?
note.title: Magnetising and demagnetising magnets
steps: For single-touch, stroke the steel bar from one end to the other several times in the same direction with the same pole, lifting the magnet at the far end.
For double-touch, stroke outwards from the centre using the unlike poles of two magnets at the same time.
For solenoid magnetisation, put the steel bar inside the solenoid and pass direct current through it; use the right-hand grip rule to identify its poles.
To demagnetise a magnet, heat it strongly, hammer it, or slowly move it out of a solenoid carrying alternating current.

This is incorrect because single-touch does not use alternating poles or back-and-forth strokes.
This is incorrect because strong heating demagnetises a magnet rather than being part of single-touch magnetising.
This is incorrect because the section uses direct current in a solenoid to magnetise the bar; A.C. is used for demagnetisation.

written.finalAnswer: Magnetic domains are small regions in a magnetic material in which the magnetic effects are aligned; when their alignment is disturbed, the material loses its magnetism.

rubric.why: This identifies what domains are and where they occur.
rubric.description: Identify domains as small regions within a magnetic material.
rubric.how: State that a magnetic material contains small regions called domains.

rubric.why: The section connects domain order or alignment with whether a material remains magnetic.

modelAnswer: Magnetic domains are small regions in a magnetic material in which the magnetic effects are aligned.
When the alignment of the domains is disturbed, the material loses its magnetism.

written.text: Why ferromagnetic materials are suitable for making magnets?
written.finalAnswer: In ferromagnetic materials, domains can align to produce magnetism and remain aligned, so the material can retain its magnetism and be made into a magnet.

rubric.why: The answer needs to explain suitability using the domain idea.
rubric.description: Refer to domains in ferromagnetic materials.
rubric.how: Name the domains as the parts whose alignment produces magnetism.

rubric.why: Domain alignment is the key link between the material and magnetism.
rubric.description: Explain that domains align to produce magnetism.
rubric.how: State that the domains can line up in an ordered direction.

rubric.why: A useful magnet must retain magnetism rather than lose it immediately.
rubric.description: Connect retained alignment with making a magnet.
rubric.how: State that the aligned domains remain aligned so the material can retain magnetism; give the final conclusion.

modelAnswer: In a ferromagnetic material, the domains can align in an ordered direction.
The domains can remain aligned, so the material retains its magnetism.
Therefore, ferromagnetic materials are suitable for making magnets.

yourTurn.question:
Q8.7. A steel rod is magnetised by double touch stroking method. Which one would be the correct polarity of the AB magnet?
The left magnet has N at its outer end and S at the end touching the bar; the right magnet has N at the end touching the bar and S at its outer end. The magnets stroke outwards from the centre.
(a) N at A, S at B
(b) S at A, N at B
(c) N at A, S in the middle, N at B
(d) S at A, N in the middle, S at B
solution: At end A, the stroking pole is S, so the pole produced at A is N.
At end B, the stroking pole is N, so the pole produced at B is S.
Therefore, A is N and B is S: option (a).
yourTurn.answer: Option (a): A is N and B is S.

explain.title: Single-touch stroking
explain.body: A steel bar is stroked several times from one end to the other in the same direction using the same pole of a permanent magnet. Lift the magnet sufficiently high after each stroke.

explain.title: Double-touch stroking
explain.body: Stroke outwards from the centre of the steel bar using the unlike poles of two permanent magnets at the same time. This method is more efficient than single-touch.

explain.title: Magnetising with a solenoid
explain.body: Place the steel bar inside a solenoid with several hundred turns of insulated copper wire. Passing direct current through the solenoid makes the bar a magnet. Use the right-hand grip rule to find its polarity.

explain.title: Demagnetising a magnet
explain.body: Strong heating or hammering disturbs the order or alignment of the domains. A magnet can also be demagnetised by slowly moving it out from inside a solenoid carrying alternating current.

mistakes: Do not mix up the currents: direct current in a solenoid magnetises the steel bar; alternating current is used to demagnetise a magnet as it is slowly withdrawn.
Do not forget to lift the magnet at the end of each single-touch stroke before returning it to the start.
In double-touch stroking, use unlike poles and stroke outwards from the centre.
Do not assign the same polarity to an end as the stroking pole; the produced pole is opposite to the stroking pole.
